text: Okay, a calculator with plus, minus, multiply and divide, no brackets. Sir, can there be spaces anywhere, and is the expression always valid? Also division truncates toward zero, so minus seven divided by two is minus three, right?

Right on the truncation, minus three is what we want, and yes, expressions are flat with no parentheses. Your question about spaces is worth answering precisely: the input can contain spaces anywhere, including around operators, so you'll want to handle them in your scan. For validity, assume it's always a well-formed expression, no need to defend against junk input.

My idea is a stack. I scan the string, build the current number digit by digit, and I remember the last operator I saw. When I hit a new operator or the end, I apply the last operator to the number: plus pushes the number, minus pushes its negative, multiply and divide pop the top and push the result. At the end I sum the stack. That's O of n time and O of n space. For division I'd do integer division.

The plan is sound, and the precedence handling via pop-and-push is the right instinct. But you said integer division, and we just agreed we want truncation toward zero. Tell me, in Python, what does integer division do for a negative numerator, and how will you correct it?

Oh right, in Python double slash floors, so minus seven double slash two is minus four, not minus three. So I should use int of a divided by b, which truncates toward zero. Float division could lose precision for huge numbers, but for this I think int of a over b is fine. Or I can do abs division and put the sign back.

That's the right catch, int of the true division truncates toward zero. Once you write it, I do want you to test one thing: a sequence like three minus five times two, so we can confirm your operator ordering is actually right. Go ahead and code it.
Okay, writing it.
Take your time. While you type, one thing to keep in mind: think about what value you add to the running total when you see a plus or minus, and when you don't. Go ahead.

Done. I keep num, op and the stack. For each character, if it's a digit I extend num. If it's an operator or the last index, I apply the previous op to num and then set op to the new operator and reset num. Division is int of pop divided by num. Then I return the sum of the stack.
Good. Let's walk through it with the one I mentioned, three minus five times two. Trace it line by line and tell me what lands in the stack and what the final sum is.

Three minus five times two. i zero is the digit three, num is three. At the minus, op is plus, so I push three and set op to minus, num to zero. Then five, num is five. At the star, op is minus, so I push minus five, and op becomes star. Then two, which is the last index, num is two, op is star, so I pop minus five, multiply by two, push minus ten. Stack is three and minus ten, the sum is minus seven. And that's right, three minus ten.

Minus seven is correct, and your ordering held: the multiply bound to the five before the minus was ever committed. Now the second trace: a string with spaces, fourteen minus three divided by two. Expect thirteen. Walk me through what's on your stack at each step.

Fourteen minus three divided by two, with spaces. The characters one and four make num fourteen, spaces are skipped because they're neither digits nor operators. At the minus, op is plus so I push fourteen, op becomes minus. Then three. At the slash, op is minus, so I push minus three, op becomes slash. Then two at the last index, op is slash, so I pop minus three, minus three divided by two is minus one point five, int of that is minus one, I push minus one. Stack is fourteen and minus one, sum is thirteen.

Thirteen, exactly right, and the truncation gave minus one as we wanted. Now, your solution is correct but it uses a stack, which is O of n extra space. Can you see a way to drop the stack entirely and keep just one running operand plus a total?

Hmm, let me think. The only element I ever pop is the top one, for multiply and divide. Everything below the top never changes again. So I could keep the sum of everything below in a variable, say total, and keep only the top as last. On plus or minus I add last into total and make last the new signed number. On star or slash I just change last. At the end I return total plus last. That's O of one space.

That's exactly the insight, and it's a real improvement, O of one space. Now tell me why it's safe: when you fold last into total on a plus or minus, why is it fine that multiply and divide can never touch that earlier part of the expression again?

Because of precedence. Multiply and divide bind tighter than plus and minus, so once I see a plus or minus, the term before it is complete, nothing later can multiply or divide into it. A star or slash only ever applies to the number right before it, which is the current last. So the earlier terms are final and can be added into total safely.

That's correct, and that's the precedence argument stated cleanly. We're at a good point here, so let's move on. I'd like to dig into your projects now. Can you walk me through the architecture decisions you made for the Next.js host shell and how you integrated the Vite React SPA remotes via Module Federation?
Let's start with the big picture then. What does the host shell own, and what does each remote own? And why did you split it that way instead of shipping one app?

Sir, I think I covered this at the start of the interview, the host owns auth, layout, design tokens and routing, and a remote is something one team can build and deploy alone. I can go deeper on one part if you want, maybe how the remotes are loaded at runtime and what happens when one is down?

Fair, you did cover the split. Pin it to something concrete. Fair, you did cover the split earlier. So let's go deeper on exactly that: how is a remote actually loaded and registered at runtime? Walk me through what happens in the host when a remote's entry is fetched, and how the host resolves which component to render.

blocked.sentence: Let's go to the part you offered then: how is a remote actually loaded and registered at runtime, and what happens when one of them is down or a version mismatches?

text: Sure. The host keeps a small config of remote names and their entry URLs. When the user opens a route, the host does a dynamic import of that remote, which fetches the remote's entry file, and the federation runtime registers its exposed modules and the shared dependencies. The route then renders the exposed component, usually wrapped in React lazy and Suspense. If a remote is down, the import rejects, an error boundary catches it, and the user sees a fallback card with a retry, while the rest of the portal still works.

That's the right picture, and the error boundary point matters. Now anchor it to one real incident. Tell me about a specific time a remote actually went down or mismatched in production. What broke, how did you detect it, and what did you change afterwards?

In production I don't have a big outage to tell you about, honestly. The closest was in staging, before launch. One remote team bumped a dependency and the remote's build changed its shared react range, and the host loaded it with a warning and one page rendered blank. We noticed from the console error on the QA environment. Afterwards I added a smoke test in CI which loads every remote's entry against the host's shared versions before a deploy.

A staging catch is still a real catch, and a cross-remote smoke test in CI is a sensible fix. Be concrete about one detail: what did that smoke test actually assert, so that a version skew like that would fail the build next time?

It loaded the host in a headless browser, mounted each remote's exposed entry, and failed if there were any console errors, like an invalid hook call, or if the remote's declared react version range didn't satisfy the host's shared version. It was a small Playwright script plus a check on the remotes' manifest. I'd say it's basic, I haven't made it catch every kind of skew.
That's concrete enough, and honest about the limits, which I like. Quick fundamentals before we wrap this part. Why must equals and hashCode be overridden together in Java?

Hash based collections like HashMap and HashSet first use hashCode to find the bucket and then equals to compare inside it. If two objects are equal by equals but give different hash codes, they can land in different buckets, so the map can't find an object that is actually there. The contract says equal objects must have equal hash codes. The other way is allowed, different objects can share a hash code, that's a collision.

That's the contract exactly, both directions covered. One more, then we can move to your questions. Write me a query for this: list the customers who have never placed an order. And tell me which join or subquery you'd pick and why.

Two ways. One is a left join: select c.id, c.name from customers c left join orders o on o.customer_id equals c.id where o.id is null. The other is not exists: select from customers c where not exists a select one from orders o where o.customer_id equals c.id. I'd pick not exists, or the left join, they usually get the same plan. I'd avoid not in with a subquery, because if the orders customer id has a null, not in returns nothing at all.
Both forms are right, and that point about null in a NOT IN subquery is genuinely important. We're near time now, so let me stop here. What questions do you have for me about the team and the work?
Thanks for your time. We'll share the feedback on the platform shortly, and you'll see the next steps there. Have a good day!
